text: In what year was the Health and Safety at Work Act passed?
explanation: The Health and Safety at Work Act was passed in 1974 and remains the primary piece of health and safety legislation in the UK.

text: What is the primary duty placed on employers under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974?

options.text: To provide employees with free health insurance
To ensure the health, safety and welfare of all employees so far as is reasonably practicable
To provide employees with a minimum wage
To install CCTV in all workplaces

explanation: Employers must ensure the health, safety and welfare of all their employees so far as is reasonably practicable — this is the core duty of the Act.

text: What does 'so far as is reasonably practicable' mean in the context of the Act?

options.text: Employers only need to act if an accident has already occurred
Employers must balance the cost and effort of safety measures against the risk involved
All possible safety measures must be implemented regardless of cost
Employers are only responsible for safety in offices, not factories

explanation: 'So far as is reasonably practicable' means employers must weigh the cost, time and effort of safety measures against the level of risk — they don't need to eliminate all risk, just reduce it to a reasonable level.

text: Which organisation enforces the Health and Safety at Work Act?

options.text: The Environment Agency
The Health and Safety Executive (HSE)
The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)
Ofcom

explanation: The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is the national regulator responsible for enforcing health and safety law in most workplaces in Great Britain.

text: What duty do employees have under the Health and Safety at Work Act?

options.text: No duty — only employers have responsibilities
To take reasonable care of their own health and safety and that of others who may be affected by their actions
To report all faults directly to the HSE
To carry out their own risk assessments

explanation: Employees also have a duty under the Act — they must take reasonable care of their own health and safety and that of others who may be affected by their work.

text: How does the Health and Safety at Work Act apply to computing professionals?

options.text: It does not apply to office-based workers
Employers must ensure safe workstations, adequate lighting, correct seating and regular breaks from screens
IT staff are exempt as their work is not physically dangerous
It only applies to hardware engineers working with electrical equipment

explanation: The Act applies to all workplaces including offices. For computing professionals this includes safe workstations, proper lighting, ergonomic seating and regular screen breaks to prevent RSI and eye strain.

text: What is RSI and how does it relate to the Health and Safety at Work Act?

options.text: Remote System Integration — a networking concept
Repetitive Strain Injury — employers must take steps to prevent it in workers who use computers for long periods
Risk and Safety Inspection — a legal requirement under the Act
Regulated Software Installation — part of IT security compliance

explanation: RSI (Repetitive Strain Injury) is a condition caused by repetitive movements such as typing. Employers must take steps to prevent it, for example by providing ergonomic equipment and rest breaks.

text: What must employers provide under the Health and Safety at Work Act?

options.text: Free meals and transport
Safe equipment, safe systems of work, information, training and supervision
A minimum of 30 days holiday per year
Private healthcare for all staff

explanation: Employers must provide safe equipment, safe systems of work, necessary information, training and supervision to ensure employee health and safety.

text: Does the Health and Safety at Work Act cover visitors and members of the public as well as employees?

options.text: No — it only covers full-time employees
Yes — employers must ensure the safety of anyone who may be affected by their work activities
Only if visitors are on site for more than one hour
Only in manufacturing and construction, not offices

explanation: The Act extends beyond employees — employers must ensure the safety of anyone who may be affected by their work activities, including visitors, contractors and members of the public.

text: What can happen to an employer who breaches the Health and Safety at Work Act?

options.text: They receive an informal warning only
They can face improvement notices, prohibition notices, fines or prosecution
They must retrain all staff
Their business licence is automatically revoked

explanation: Breaches can result in improvement notices, prohibition notices (stopping unsafe activities), unlimited fines and even prosecution leading to imprisonment for serious cases.

text: What is a risk assessment in the context of health and safety?

options.text: A financial review of business costs
A systematic examination of a workplace to identify hazards and evaluate the risk they pose to workers
A software tool used to monitor employee performance
An annual report submitted to the HSE

explanation: A risk assessment systematically examines the workplace to identify hazards and evaluate the risks they pose — employers use them to determine what safety measures are needed.

text: Which regulations, made under the Health and Safety at Work Act, specifically cover display screen equipment used by computer workers?

options.text: The WEEE Regulations
The Display Screen Equipment (DSE) Regulations
The Data Protection Act
The Working Time Regulations

explanation: The Display Screen Equipment (DSE) Regulations were made under the Health and Safety at Work Act and specifically require employers to assess workstations and ensure safe use of computer screens.

text: A software developer complains of wrist pain after months of typing. What should their employer do under the Health and Safety at Work Act?

options.text: Nothing — minor discomfort is not covered by the Act
Carry out a workstation assessment and provide ergonomic equipment and rest breaks to prevent further injury
Ask the employee to work from home instead
Report the incident to the police

explanation: The employer must take action — carrying out a workstation assessment and providing appropriate equipment and breaks. Ignoring the complaint could constitute a breach of the Act.

text: What is the significance of the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 for the IT industry specifically?

options.text: It requires all IT equipment to be CE marked
It ensures IT workers are protected from work-related injuries such as eye strain, back problems and RSI caused by prolonged computer use
It sets data security standards for IT companies
It requires IT companies to maintain fire safety systems

explanation: For the IT industry the Act is significant because it protects workers from conditions caused by prolonged computer use — including eye strain, back and neck problems, and RSI from keyboard and mouse use.

text: Under the Health and Safety at Work Act, can an employee refuse to carry out work they believe is unsafe?

options.text: No — employees must follow all instructions from their employer
Yes — employees have the right to stop work they reasonably believe poses serious and imminent danger
Only if they have written permission from a union representative
Only in construction and manufacturing, not in computing

explanation: Employees have the right to stop work they reasonably believe poses serious and imminent danger — they cannot be penalised for doing so under health and safety law.
